::: {#def-row-vector-derivative}
#### Row-vector derivative (total derivative)
If $f(\vcoef)$ is a scalar-valued function of a $p \times 1$ vector $\vcoef$,
such as $f(\vcoef) = \tp{\vx}\vcoef$,
then its **row-vector derivative** is the row vector of its
partial derivatives (@def-partial-derivative):

$$
\derivf{f(\vcoef)}{\tp{\vcoef}} =
\sbmat{
\deriv{\coef{1}}f(\vcoef) &
\deriv{\coef{2}}f(\vcoef) &
\cdots &
\deriv{\coef{p}}f(\vcoef)
}
$$ {#eq-row-vector-derivative}

Some sources write the same row vector as $\deriv{\tp{\vcoef}} f(\vcoef)$,
with the operator on the left,
read as each operator $\deriv{\coef{i}}$ applied to $f$ rather than as a matrix product
(see @rem-row-derivative-shape).

The row-vector derivative is also called the **total derivative** of $f$,
the name used when the derivative of a scalar-valued function is written as a row vector.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-row-derivative-shape}
#### Which side the operator goes on

Read $\deriv{\vcoef}$ as a $p \times 1$ column vector of operators
with entries $\deriv{\coef{1}}, \ldots, \deriv{\coef{p}}$,
and $\deriv{\tp{\vcoef}}$ as the $1 \times p$ row vector of operators with the same entries.
Writing either one next to $f$ can be read in two ways:

- **As a matrix product,**
  with $f$ a $1 \times 1$ matrix,
  under the shape rule of [matrix multiplication](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-mult).
  The column-vector operator works on the left:
  $\deriv{\vcoef} f$ is $(p \times 1)(1 \times 1)$, a $p \times 1$ column vector (@def-vector-derivative).
  The row-vector operator does not:
  $\deriv{\tp{\vcoef}} f$ is $(1 \times p)(1 \times 1)$,
  whose inner dimensions $p$ and $1$ do not match when $p > 1$.
  For the shape rule to give the $1 \times p$ row vector,
  the operator would have to go on the right of $f$, as in $(1 \times 1)(1 \times p)$,
  which changes its meaning (see below).
- **As a scalar multiple,**
  with $f$ a scalar,
  the way $c \vx$ is read in [scalar multiplication](linear-algebra.qmd#def-scalar-mult),
  which has no shape rule:
  each entry of the operator vector is applied to $f$.
  Then both $\deriv{\vcoef} f$ and $\deriv{\tp{\vcoef}} f$ work with the operator on the left.

The fraction $\derivf{f}{\tp{\vcoef}}$ of @eq-row-vector-derivative
means the same thing under both readings:
the transpose in the denominator says the result is a row vector,
without making the derivative a product.

Treating the operators as vectors is sound for checking shapes,
but "multiplying" an operator by a function means applying the operator to it,
so two rules of ordinary matrix algebra do not carry over:
scalars commute with matrices, and products can be regrouped.

- **Scalars do not commute with operators.**
  $\deriv{\coef{i}} f$ is a function,
  but $f \deriv{\coef{i}}$ is still an unapplied operator, waiting for something to act on.
  So, unlike $c \vx = \vx c$, the operator cannot move to the other side of $f$
  without changing the meaning.
  Putting the row-vector operator on the right of $f$ gives the row-vector derivative
  only under the convention that it acts on the factor to its left.
- **Products cannot be regrouped.**
  An operator acts on the whole product to its right,
  so by the [product rule](calculus.qmd#thm-product-rule),
  $\deriv{\coef{i}} (f g) \ne \paren{\deriv{\coef{i}} f} g$ in general.
  For example, with $f(\vcoef) = \coef{1}$,
  $\deriv{\coef{1}} (f f) = 2 \coef{1}$
  but $\paren{\deriv{\coef{1}} f} f = \coef{1}$.

:::
